answer_text:
Assume \(n\in\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\dots\}\). The exponent
\[
(-n)^n=(-1)^n n^n
\]
is always an integer, so the powers are ordinary integer powers.

Split by parity.

**If \(n\) is even**, then \((-n)^n=n^n\) is a positive even integer, so
\[
a_n=(-n)^{n^n}=n^{n^n}.
\]
Along the even subsequence,
\[
a_n\to +\infty.
\]

**If \(n\) is odd**, then \((-n)^n=-n^n\) is a negative odd integer, so
\[
a_n=(-n)^{-n^n}=-\frac1{n^{n^n}}.
\]
Along the odd subsequence,
\[
a_n\to 0.
\]

Thus \(0\) is a limit point. Any finite limit point must come from a subsequence converging to a real number. Since the even terms go to \(+\infty\), a finite-convergent subsequence can contain only finitely many even terms; its odd terms then force the limit to be \(0\). Hence no other real limit points exist.

Therefore, in the usual real sense, the set of limit points is

\[
\boxed{\{0\}}
\]

If one works in the extended real line, then \(+\infty\) is also an accumulation point.
